Since 1974

We have never
sold anything twice.

Every garment that passes through Marchmont Row is bought by hand, one at a time, from estate sales, house clearances and the occasional astonishing wardrobe. There is no second size, no restock, no next season.

What arrives is washed or dry-cleaned by a specialist, repaired where repair is honest, measured flat, photographed and described without flattery. If a seam has been restitched, we say so.

        Home  /  Our Story

        Fifty years
        on the row.

        Margaret Hollis opened a single room above a bookbinder in 1974 with eleven coats and a steamer. The shop has moved twice since, both times by about forty feet.

        The premise

        Nothing here was made
        to be replaced.

        For most of the twentieth century, a coat was a considered purchase. It was cut from cloth chosen for how it would behave in ten years, sewn by someone who expected to be judged on the inside of the garment as much as the outside, and repaired rather than discarded.

        That assumption produced clothes that are still, decades later, better than most of what is made now. Our entire business is the small, unglamorous work of finding those clothes, putting them right, and passing them on.

        We are not nostalgic about it. Some vintage is badly made, badly stored and not worth the rail space. We buy perhaps one garment in forty that we are shown.

        How it works

        From doorstep to rail

        One

        We are shown a wardrobe

        Estate sales, house clearances, a phone call from a family sorting through a life. Two of us go, in person, with a tape measure and a torch. We look at seams, linings, moth damage and the inside of cuffs before we look at labels.

        Two

        It is cleaned by a specialist

        Wool is brushed and steamed. Silk goes to a hand-finisher we have used since 1988. Leather is fed and rested. Nothing goes near a solvent unless the cloth genuinely requires it, because forty years of dry cleaning is what kills a good jacket.

        Three

        It is repaired, not restored

        A failing seam is restitched in matching thread. A missing button is replaced from the button drawer, which has been filling since the seventies. A worn elbow stays a worn elbow — that is the garment’s biography, and erasing it would be a kind of lie.

        Four

        It is measured and described

        Laid flat on the bench and measured in inches: chest, shoulder, sleeve, length. Condition is graded and the flaws are named first. Then it is photographed as it is, without a filter that flatters the colour.

        Five

        It is priced once

        We price against what the piece is, not what the label shouts. There are no seasonal sales, because a garment that has survived sixty years does not become less good in January.

        “A good coat should be the least interesting decision you make all decade.”
        Elias Vane, partner since 1991

        Grading

        What our condition
        words actually mean.

        Excellent. No visible flaws at conversational distance or closer. Original hardware. Ready to wear the day it arrives.

        Very good. Honest wear consistent with age — a softened cuff, a flattened nap, a patina on brass. Structurally sound throughout.

        Good. One named flaw we have decided is worth living with, always described and photographed. Priced accordingly.

        We do not list anything below good. If it cannot be worn, it is not stock.

        Notes from

        Things worth knowing before you buy anything old — written by the people who mend it.

        Tailoring · 6 min · March

        How to read a jacket before you try it on

        Almost everything you need to know about a jacket is visible while it is still on the hanger. Start with the shoulder. A good one follows the line of a real body: a slight, soft roll where the sleeve head meets the shoulder seam, no dimpling, no rigid pad holding a shape the wearer does not have. If the shoulder is wrong, nothing a tailor does will save it. It is the one measurement that cannot be altered.

        Then the lapel. Roll it back with your thumb. A canvassed jacket has a lapel with a gentle, three-dimensional curve that returns when released; a fused jacket has a lapel that creases flat like a card. Fusing fails eventually — it bubbles, and there is no repair. Half-canvassed is the honest middle ground and covers most of what we sell.

        Look at the buttonholes next. Hand-worked holes have a slightly irregular, dense gimp and a tiny keyhole that flares toward the edge. Machine holes are perfectly even. Neither is a flaw, but hand-worked holes tell you the rest of the jacket was probably made with the same patience.

        Finally, the inside. A maker’s ticket in the breast pocket, often with a date and a customer name, is the closest thing tailoring has to a birth certificate. Check the seam allowances while you are in there: a generous allowance means the jacket can be let out, which means a jacket that fits nearly right is a jacket that will fit exactly right for about eighty pounds.

        Shop tailoring →

        Cloth · 8 min · February

        Selvedge, hidden rivets, and other honest tells

        Denim is the most counterfeited category in vintage, largely because the people who care about it care very much and the details are small. Fortunately, the tells are physical rather than cosmetic, and a reproduction rarely bothers with all of them.

        Turn the outseam out. A narrow shuttle loom finishes its own edge, and that finished edge — the selvedge — appears as a clean, tightly woven band, usually with a coloured line running through it. Wide modern looms cannot produce it; a serged, overlocked outseam means the denim was woven after roughly 1980, whatever the label says.

        Then the back pockets. Through the 1940s and into the 1960s, rivets at the back pocket corners were placed under the fabric rather than on top, to stop them destroying saddles and chair seats. From the outside you see only a faint circular impression. It is an inconvenient detail to fake and a reliable one to trust.

        Fades are the last thing to read, and the hardest to forge convincingly. Genuine wear concentrates where a body creases the cloth: honeycombs behind the knee, whiskers at the hip, a wallet outline that no laundry has removed. The pattern is asymmetric, because people are. Uniform, symmetrical fading is a factory pretending to be a decade.

        Shop trousers & denim →

        Care · 5 min · January

        The case against dry cleaning almost everything

        Dry cleaning is a solvent bath followed by heat and mechanical agitation. It is very good at removing oil-based stains and quite good at removing the natural oils that keep wool fibres flexible. Do it four times a year for a decade and you will have a jacket that looks thin at the elbows and feels like paper, which is exactly what has happened to most of the mid-century tailoring we are shown.

        For wool, the answer is almost always air and a brush. Hang the garment somewhere with moving air for a day after wearing it; most odour is volatile and simply leaves. Brush with a natural-bristle clothes brush, always downward, to lift the dust that abrades fibres from within. Steam — a kettle, a bathroom, a hand steamer held at a distance — releases creases without pressing shine into the cloth.

        Spot-clean rather than committing the whole garment. A damp cloth, cold water and patience will take out more than people expect, and a specialist can treat a single mark for a fraction of what a full clean costs the fabric.

        Send a piece for cleaning when it is genuinely soiled, at the end of a season before storage, or when a stain has set. That is perhaps once every two or three years. Between times, the best thing you can do for an old coat is hang it on a broad wooden hanger and leave it alone.

        Selling to us

        Have you found
        a wardrobe?

        We buy outright, in cash, and we travel. Tailoring, outerwear, knitwear, leather goods and evening wear from roughly 1930 to 1990 are of most interest; so is anything with a maker’s ticket still in the pocket.

        Send half a dozen photographs — the whole garment, the label, the inside of a cuff, and anything you think is damage — and we will tell you honestly whether it is something we can use. If it is, we will come to you.

        Email the buying desk

        Practicalities

        Questions we get

        Every listing carries measurements taken with the garment laid flat, in inches. The reliable method is to measure something you already own and wear happily, and compare. If you are between two of our numbers, write to us — after fifty years we have a fair sense of which cuts run generous.

        Complimentary on orders over $300. A flat $18 otherwise. Everything is dispatched within two working days, steamed and wrapped in acid-free tissue, tracked and signed for. International shipping is quoted at cost before we take payment.

        Fourteen days from delivery, unworn, with the tag still attached. We pay the return label within the UK. Because every piece is one of one, we cannot exchange — a return is a refund, and the garment goes back on the rail.

        Yes. Our tailor works from the back room on Wednesdays and Fridays. Sleeves shortened, trousers tapered, waists taken in, hems raised. Ask for a quote before you buy and we will tell you what is possible in the seam allowance — and, occasionally, that it is not worth doing.

        Yes. There is no back stock and no restock. When a listing sells it comes down, and the only way we would ever have the same garment again is if you sold it back to us — which, for the record, several people have.

        For twenty-four hours, gladly, and longer if you are travelling to the shop to see it. Write or telephone. We would rather a coat went to someone who has looked at it properly.
